title: Yanzick,Kathleen J, Crime Victim Order
text:
64 Van Natta 504 (2012) 504
In the Matter of the Compensation of
KATHLEEN J. YANZICK, Applicant
WCB Case No. 11-00006CV
ORDER ON REVIEW (CRIME VICTIMS’ ACT) (REMANDING)
Unrepresented Claimant
Department of Justice, Defense Attorneys
Reviewing Panel: Members Lowell and Biehl.
Applicant has requested review by the Workers’ Compensation Board
(Board) of a Determination Order dated March 2, 2011, as reconsidered on
September 15, 2011, issued by the Department of Justice Crime Victims’
Assistance Section (Department). By its orders, the Department denied
compensation to applicant under the Compensation of Crime Victims Act (Act),
ORS Chapter 147. The Department based its denial on findings that, without
“good cause,” applicant failed to cooperate with law enforcement officials in
the apprehension and prosecution of the assailants.
Following our receipt of the request for Board review, the Department
was directed to file a certified copy of the entire record together with an index
and to mail a certified copy of the record to applicant within 15 days.1 OAR
438-082-0025(2). In addition, applicant was advised that she could present her
case to a hearing officer. Applicant was also notified that, if no hearing was
requested, she could submit written argument. The Department was also provided
the opportunity to submit written argument.
Applicant did not request a hearing and submitted no additional written
argument beyond that presented with her request for review.2 The Department
also did not submit any written argument. The deadline for submission of such
written arguments has passed; therefore, we conduct our review based on the
written record and applicant’s request for review.
Following our review of the written record, we conclude that remand is
appropriate. We reason as follows.
1 This record was timely received on January 6, 2012.
2 Although not submitting any additional written argument, applicant submitted written
notification of the correct date of birth of her sister, Barbara Yanzick. That information is also in the
record submitted by the Department. (Ex. 7B-1).

64 Van Natta 504 (2012) 505
The standard for our review under the Act is de novo, based on the entire
record. ORS 147.155(5); Jill M. Gabriel, 35 Van Natta 1224, 1226 (1983).
ORS 147.015 provides that a person is eligible for crime victims’
compensation if, among other requirements:
“(3) The applicant has cooperated fully with law
enforcement officials in the apprehension and
prosecution of the assailant or the department has found
that the applicant’s failure to cooperate was for good
cause[.]”
Thus, ORS 147.015(3) provides an exception to the requirement to fully
cooperate with law enforcement officials in the apprehension and prosecution of
the assailant(s). Such exception is predicated on the Department finding “good
cause” for failure to fully cooperate. Moreover, the Department has adopted rules
that define “failure to cooperate” and “good cause” under this situation.
Specifically, OAR 137-076-0010 provides, in relevant part:
“(3) ‘Failure to Cooperate’ means any act or omission by
a victim that prejudices a law enforcement agency in the
timely investigation of a crime or which causes the
agency to abandon its investigation, or which prejudices
a prosecuting official in a timely prosecution of the crime
or causes or contributes to a decision by the official to
abandon prosecution.
“(4) ‘Good Cause for Failure to Cooperate’ exists when
the victim receives express or implied threats that
cooperation will result in death or serious physical injury
to the victim or another person and that these expressed
or implied threats can be documented by the Program.”
Here, in issuing its March 2, 2011 Determination Order, the Department
relied on applicant’s October 12, 2010 Crime Victim Compensation Application
form, the May 25, 2010 Portland Police Bureau Investigation Report, and the
May 25, 2010 hospital emergency room report. (Exs. 6B-2, 7B, 8B, 2D). All
of these documents were included in the certified record submitted by the
Department.

64 Van Natta 504 (2012) 506
Based on these documents, the Department made the following findings.
On May 25, 2010, after applicant retrieved the mail and entered the house, her
sister, Barbara, tried to grab the mail from her, resulting in a physical altercation
between the sisters. Applicant reported that after her sister assaulted her, her
sister’s son,3 Nathaniel, who is autistic, grabbed her by the throat and bit her.
Applicant was treated at the emergency room, where she was diagnosed with a
one centimeter scalp laceration secondary to a “human bite.” At the emergency
room, applicant told police that she only wanted to document the incident because
she did not wish to file a complaint against her sister or nephew. (Ex. 6B-2).
The Department reasoned that, as a result of applicant’s “choice to not
file a complaint against her sister, her sister shall never face prosecution and be
personally held accountable for causing [applicant’s] pain, suffering and financial
costs via the criminal court.” (Ex. 6B-3). The Department concluded that
applicant failed to cooperate with police without good cause. ORS 147.015(3);
OAR 137-076-0010(3), (4).
Applicant requested reconsideration, arguing, in part, that she “did
everything in [her] power to fully cooperate with law enforcement – messages
were left several times with little response.” (Ex. 5B-1).
On September 15, 2011, the Department issued a Reconsideration Order,
continuing to find that applicant failed to cooperate with police without good
cause. In reaching this conclusion, the Department relied, in part, on evidence
that is not in the record. Specifically, the Department held:
“Information received by the Department indicates that
[applicant] did call the Portland Police Bureau on two
different occasions requesting the original reporting
officer meet with her; however[,] during her
conversations with police [applicant] would not relay the
information to the officer over the telephone. [Applicant]
was then informed that she would need to travel to the
East Precinct or call 911 to document the information.
[Applicant] did not follow through with the officer’s
instructions and the information was never documented.”
(Ex. 4B-2).
3 Although the Determination Order listed Nathaniel’s age as seven, the Department’s
September 15, 2011 Reconsideration Order noted that he was seventeen years old. (Ex. 4B-1).

64 Van Natta 504 (2012) 507
The record contains no evidence regarding this “[i]nformation received by
the Department.” As addressed above, the standard for our review under the Act
is de novo, based on the entire record. ORS 147.155(5); Gabriel, 35 Van
Natta at 1226. Moreover, we are empowered to conduct proceedings in any
manner that will achieve substantial justice. ORS 147.155(5).
Here, the determinative issue is whether applicant fully cooperated with law
enforcement officials in the apprehension and prosecution of her assailants and, if
not, whether she established good cause for failing to do so. See ORS 147.015(3);
OAR 137-076-0010(3), (4). Because the record does not include documentary
evidence that the Department apparently relied on in reaching its decision
regarding this issue, we are unable to perform our de novo review of the entire
record.4
Under such circumstances, we conclude that substantial justice would be
served by remanding this matter to the Department. In reaching this conclusion,
we emphasize that we are not passing judgment on the merits of applicant’s claim
for benefits. Rather, we are merely holding that, in the interests of substantial
justice, the Department should consider whether this record is complete before
it reaches its decision regarding the application for benefits.5
Accordingly, this matter is remanded to the Department for further action
consistent with this order. Thereafter, the Department shall issue a reconsideration
order. Should applicant continue to disagree with the Department’s decision
following its reconsideration order, she may again petition the Board for review
of the Department’s reconsideration order.
IT IS SO ORDERED.
Entered at Salem, Oregon on March 9, 2012
4 Although not apparent from this record, it is possible that the information that the Department
relied on may have been received by means of a telephone conversation with Portland police officers.
If that is the case, a memo, message, or phone log summarizing such conversation should have been
included in the record to document that event. Without such documentation, the corresponding “finding”
contained in the Department’s order regarding this interaction is not supported by the record.
5 Our decision also should not be interpreted as a limitation on the evidence to be considered on
remand. To the contrary, the Department may proceed in whatever manner it deems appropriate in
further investigating this application before arriving at its ultimate decision. Likewise, if applicant has
additional information, she should present such written materials to the Department for its consideration.
